title: Insurance Is a Balance-Sheet Decision, Not a Purchase
summary: Your ability to earn, sign and lead is the largest asset on your balance sheet in the early years, and it appears on no statement. Life, disability and key-person cover exist to protect that asset and the obligations that depend on it. This lesson, with Priya, frames insurance as architecture rather than a product.
body:
The largest asset you own today is probably not a building. It is your capacity to earn, sign, decide and lead for the next twenty years. Insurance architecture decides what happens to everyone who depends on that asset if it stops working.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between a fiduciary duty and a suitability standard?

A. A fiduciary must act in the client's interest and avoid or manage conflicts. A suitability standard only requires that a recommendation fit the client, so among suitable options the adviser may choose the one that pays them more.

Q. In position sizing, what sets the size of a position?

A. The loss you can bear on it without changing your life or your other obligations. The upside is judged inside that limit.

Q. In a risk register, what two numbers rank a risk?

A. Its probability and its impact. Each risk also needs a named owner, a trigger that says when to act, and a planned response.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in Week 80 Roman taught you to build a risk register for a project. This week you build one for yourself. A developer's early career is unusually exposed: one person carries the relationships, the guarantees, the signing authority and the vision. Lenders know this, which is why many loan agreements name key principals and treat their death or incapacity as a serious event. Partners know it too. If you cannot work for a year, the building does not stop needing decisions. Insurance is the tool that turns that concentrated, uninsurable-by-diversification risk into a defined, paid-for cost.

Priya joins today because the lender sees this risk before you do, and often asks for insurance as a condition of the loan.

Human capital: the asset on no statement

In plain English: human capital is the value of everything you will earn from your work in the future, counted today.

The professional framing treats it like any income stream: forecast it, discount it for time and risk, and you have a present value. Early in a career it often dwarfs financial assets. Late in a career most of it has been converted into financial wealth, and it shrinks. That curve is why insurance needs usually fall over time: the asset being protected is being turned into money that can protect itself.

A worked example, hypothetical round numbers. A developer expects to earn 200,000 dollars a year for 20 more years. Ignoring growth and discounting at 5 percent a year, the present value of that stream is about 2,490,000 dollars. Their investable assets total 600,000 dollars. On paper, the person has 600,000 dollars of wealth. In reality, about 80 percent of their economic value is the ability to keep working. A balance sheet that ignores it misreads where the risk lives.

The three questions insurance answers

In plain English: insurance architecture asks what happens if you die, what happens if you cannot work, and what happens to the business if either occurs.

The professional framing assigns a cover to each question. Life insurance pays a sum on death. It comes in two broad shapes: term insurance, which covers a fixed period and has no savings element, and permanent insurance, which is designed to last for life and usually builds a cash value, at a much higher premium. Disability insurance replaces part of your income if illness or injury stops you working, and is defined by what counts as disabled, how long you wait before benefits start and how long they last. Key-person insurance is owned by a company on the life or health of a person whose loss would hurt the company, and pays the company, not the family.

A common error is to buy only life cover. For a person of working age, the probability of a long disability before retirement is generally considered meaningfully higher than the probability of death in the same period, and a disabled person still has living costs. Verify current statistics with a licensed adviser before you rely on any figure.

Say that out loud now.

Key-person risk is a lender's risk and a partner's risk

In plain English: if the business depends on one person, that person's loss can break the loan, the partnership and the project together.

The professional framing names three exposures. First, credit: a loan agreement may contain a key-principal clause, making death or incapacity an event that requires a replacement acceptable to the lender. Second, ownership: if a partner dies, their shares pass to their estate, and the survivors may suddenly co-own the company with heirs who never chose to be developers. A buy-sell agreement sets out who buys those shares and at what price, but an agreement to buy is worthless without the money to buy. Third, operations: the relationships, approvals and knowledge in one person's head take time and money to replace.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Two partners each own half of a development company worth 4,000,000 dollars. Their buy-sell agreement says the survivor buys the deceased partner's half at fair value. That is 2,000,000 dollars, due within months. Neither partner holds 2,000,000 dollars in cash. Insurance on each partner, sized to the buyout and owned in the way the agreement requires, turns an impossible obligation into a funded one. The structure, who owns the policy and who receives the money, has tax and legal consequences that a lawyer and tax adviser must design; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Insurance as architecture, not purchase

A purchase answers "which policy should I buy?" Architecture answers "which obligations would fail, in what order, if I died or could not work, and what funds each one?" Start from the obligations: the household, the guarantees, the buyout, the loan's key-principal clause, the time to replace you. Then decide which can be carried by reserves, which by insurance, and which by changing the structure so the obligation does not exist. Insurance is one answer among three.

The Six-Lens Check

Omar's six lenses on insurance architecture. Tax: premiums and proceeds can be treated very differently depending on who owns the policy and why; verify that against the primary source. Liability: proceeds paid to a company may be reachable by that company's creditors, so ownership matters. Banking: a lender may require key-person cover and an assignment of the policy. Governance: the board, not one partner, should approve policies the company owns. Estate: beneficiary designations can override a will, so they must be coordinated with it. Exit: on a sale of the company, policies on departing partners must be dealt with deliberately.

A licensed adviser is required before you act. This lesson teaches concepts; it recommends no insurer, policy or product.

Professional sign-off required: licensed insurance adviser, lawyer and tax adviser.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an obligation that depends on your continued life and health with nothing to fund it: a guarantee, a buyout, a household, a key-principal clause. The control is a written map of every such obligation, with its funding source, reviewed whenever a new loan, partner or dependant is added.

The beginner's mistake

Buying a policy because someone offered one, sized to a round number, without first listing the obligations it is meant to fund. A policy without a job is either too small or too expensive.

Callback

In Week 8, Tessa and Warrick taught the base: a will, powers of attorney, insurance and emergency reserves. That lesson covered the person. This week extends it to the business and the lender, because a developer's obligations do not stop at the family; they run through every signature he has given.

Recap

Human capital is your largest early asset and appears on no statement. Life, disability and key-person cover answer three different questions. Key-person risk touches the loan, the partnership and operations at once. Start from obligations, then choose reserves, insurance or restructuring.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of a partner's death, an unfunded buyout and a loan in default.
checklist: I have estimated my human capital and compared it with my financial assets.
I have listed every obligation that depends on my life or health.
Each obligation has a funding source: reserves, insurance or restructuring.
I know whether my loans contain a key-principal clause.
Every buy-sell agreement I am party to is funded, not just signed.
I have considered disability, not only death.
Beneficiary designations are coordinated with my will.
A licensed adviser, lawyer and tax adviser have reviewed the design.
head: Field checklist
speak: Early in a career, the largest asset I own is my ability to earn, sign and lead, my human capital. On hypothetical numbers, 200,000 dollars a year for 20 years is worth about 2.5 million today, often far more than my investments. Insurance architecture asks three questions. What happens if I die? That is life insurance, either term for a fixed period or permanent for life at a higher cost. What happens if I cannot work? That is disability insurance, often more likely than death during a working life. What happens to the business? That is key-person insurance, owned by and paid to the company. Key-person risk hits the loan, through key-principal clauses, the partnership, through buy-sell agreements that need money to work, and operations. I start from obligations, not products, and decide which are funded by reserves, insurance or restructuring, with licensed advisers designing the detail.
terms: Human capital — the present value of all future earnings from a person's work.
Term insurance — life insurance that covers a fixed period and pays only if death occurs within it.
Key-person insurance — insurance owned by and payable to a company on a person whose loss would harm the company.

hostile.q: Your company has one decision-maker who signs every guarantee and holds every relationship. If you are hit by a truck next month, how does my loan get repaid?
hostile.a: That is exactly the risk I have mapped. The company holds key-person life and disability cover on me sized to the loan exposure and the cost of replacing me, and I am prepared to assign it to you to the extent of the debt. We also have a named deputy with documented authority and a written succession plan for the project. I can show you the policy schedule and the plan.

title: The Buy-Sell Nobody Funded
summary: This is a composite example. Two partners signed a buy-sell agreement and a construction loan with a key-principal clause, then one died mid-build. With no insurance behind either document, the survivor faced a lender demand and a buyout he could not pay. Taken through seven steps, it gives Rule 88.
rule: Rule 88: Before any loan closes, every death or disability that would trigger a default, a buyout or a lost guarantee must be funded by insurance or reserves, and the funding must be tied in writing to the document that needs it.
body:
This is a composite example. Two partners did everything a careful lawyer would ask on paper and nothing on the money, so when one of them died, the paper created obligations that no one could pay.

Recall

Q. In the Day 5 portfolio example last week, what was the net return after all costs?

A. 6.80 percent gross minus 1.41 percent of total costs, which is 5.39 percent a year, on hypothetical numbers.

Q. How is concentration measured?

A. As a share of net worth exposed to one asset, sponsor or risk driver, not as a dollar amount. What matters is whether one failure would change your life.

Q. In a risk register, why must each risk have an owner?

A. Because a risk that belongs to everyone belongs to no one. The owner watches the trigger and carries out the response.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this failure is told in a lender's language and a family's at the same time. It is a composite, assembled from patterns that recur in closely held real estate companies; the numbers are hypothetical round figures. Nobody in it was reckless. Each document was sensible. The failure was that the documents and the money were never connected.

1. Timeline

Two partners form a development company, each owning half. They sign a shareholder agreement with a buy-sell clause: on the death of either, the survivor must buy the deceased's shares at a fair value fixed by a formula, payable within twelve months. They start a 25,000,000 dollar residential project with a construction loan. The loan agreement names both as key principals and makes the death or incapacity of either an event requiring a replacement acceptable to the lender within 90 days, failing which it becomes an event of default. Both sign personal completion and cost-overrun guarantees. In month 14 of construction, one partner dies suddenly. The company is worth, by the formula, 6,000,000 dollars, so the buyout price is 3,000,000 dollars. The survivor has about 400,000 dollars of liquid assets. No life insurance was in place on either partner.

2. Key decisions

The partners decided to sign a buy-sell clause without funding it. They decided to accept a key-principal clause without negotiating what a replacement must look like or how long they would have. They each decided to give personal guarantees without considering what happens to a guarantee when the guarantor dies. Each decision was taken in a different meeting with a different adviser, and nobody owned the whole picture.

3. Assumptions

They assumed they had time, because they were healthy and in their forties. They assumed insurance could be bought later, when the company was bigger. They assumed the lender would be flexible if something happened. They assumed the estate would be patient about the buyout. Each assumption was about other people's behaviour under stress, and each one turned out wrong.

4. Incentives

The deceased partner's estate had a duty to its beneficiaries to collect the buyout price promptly and to seek release from the guarantees, which bind the estate. The lender's credit committee had to protect its exposure, and a loan without one of its two key principals is a weaker loan. The survivor needed time, money and a cooperative co-owner, and had none of the three. Every party acted reasonably for itself, which is exactly why the outcome was bad.

5. Warning signs ignored

Roman's list. The buy-sell clause specified a price and a deadline but no source of funds. The loan agreement's key-principal clause was flagged by the borrower's lawyer at closing, and set aside as standard. The partners' accountant had once suggested key-person cover in a year-end letter. The company's balance sheet showed rising value, which raised the buyout price every year while the survivors' cash did not keep up. A rising price for an unfunded obligation is a growing hole.

Say that out loud now.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was day 90 after the death. No replacement principal acceptable to the lender had been agreed, because the survivor could not show how the company would be owned and controlled, with an unpaid buyout hanging over it. The lender declared an event of default, which allowed it to stop funding draws. With construction mid-way, the contractor slowed work, and the cost of delay began to compound. From there the realistic options were a forced recapitalisation on poor terms or a sale of the project half-built.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a gap between obligations and funding. The partners created three obligations triggered by death, the buyout, the key-principal replacement and the guarantees, and funded none of them. Insurance on each partner, sized to the buyout plus the guarantee exposure plus the cost of replacement, would have put cash into the company within weeks, let the survivor buy the shares, given the lender a credible plan and let the estate be released cleanly.

How it ends, in this composite

The survivor brings in an outside equity partner at a steep discount to fund the buyout and satisfy the lender, giving away a large share of the future profit. The estate is paid late and only after legal costs on both sides. The project finishes over budget because of the delay. Nobody committed a wrong; the absence of one funded decision cost all of them.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing documents with death or disability triggers in separate meetings, so no one sees that together they demand money that does not exist. The control is a single obligations map, reviewed before every closing, listing each trigger, the amount it demands, the deadline and the funding source.

The beginner's mistake

Treating a buy-sell agreement as finished once it is signed. It is a promise to pay. A promise to pay with no source of money is a lawsuit waiting for a date.

The prevention rule

Rule 88: Before any loan closes, every death or disability that would trigger a default, a buyout or a lost guarantee must be funded by insurance or reserves, and the funding must be tied in writing to the document that needs it.

Callback

In Week 69, JAX and LEX taught partner agreements: vesting, deadlock, drag and tag, and the three Ds of death, disability and divorce. That lesson wrote the clauses. This case shows what a clause is worth when the money behind it was never arranged. The clause decides who must pay; only funding decides whether they can.

Recap

A buy-sell clause, a key-principal clause and personal guarantees each created a death-triggered obligation. None was funded. Day 90 passed, the loan defaulted and the survivor recapitalised at a discount. Rule 88 ties every such trigger to its funding before closing.

Next: Priya, with Warrick, on The Money: what key-person risk does to a loan, and what insurance really costs against what it protects.
checklist: I keep one obligations map listing every death or disability trigger I have signed.
Each trigger shows the amount demanded, the deadline and the funding source.
Every buy-sell agreement names how the buyout is funded.
I have negotiated what a replacement principal must look like and how long we have.
I know what happens to each personal guarantee if I die.
The map is reviewed before every loan closing and every new partner.
Insurance ownership and beneficiaries match what each agreement requires.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite example. Two equal partners signed a buy-sell clause requiring the survivor to buy a deceased partner's shares within a year, a construction loan with a key-principal clause giving 90 days to find an acceptable replacement, and personal guarantees. Mid-construction, one partner died. The buyout price was 3 million dollars; the survivor had 400,000. No insurance existed. The estate needed paying and wanted out of the guarantees, the lender needed a credible plan, and the survivor had neither money nor time. On day 90 the lender declared a default and stopped funding draws. The survivor recapitalised at a steep discount. The root cause was obligations created by death with no funding behind any of them. Rule 88: before any loan closes, every death or disability trigger must be funded by insurance or reserves, tied in writing to the document that needs it.
terms: Buy-sell agreement — a contract fixing who must buy an owner's shares, and at what price, on events such as death or disability.
Key-principal clause — a loan provision treating the death, incapacity or departure of a named person as an event requiring lender approval of a replacement.
Event of default — a defined failure under a loan agreement that allows the lender to stop funding and enforce its remedies.

hostile.q: Your shareholder agreement obliges the survivor to buy out a deceased partner within twelve months. Where does that money come from?
hostile.a: From insurance owned in the way the agreement requires, sized to the current formula price plus a margin for growth, reviewed every year when the valuation is updated. I can show you the policy schedule against the buy-sell price. If the value has outgrown the cover, that is flagged on our obligations map and we increase it before the next closing.

title: What Key-Person Risk Costs a Loan, and What Insurance Costs to Fix It
summary: Lenders price the risk that a project depends on one person, through clauses, reserves and terms. This lesson compares that cost with the premium for cover, shows how a policy can protect debt service, and closes with Warrick's Wealth Ledger and how large firms manage key-person risk.
body:
Key-person risk has a price whether or not you insure it. Either you pay a premium to transfer it, or you carry it in worse loan terms, bigger reserves and the chance of a default at the worst moment.

Recall

Q. In last week's product pitch, what three facts did Warrick insist on before any decision?

A. How the adviser is paid, the total annual cost in dollars, and who holds and values the assets.

Q. What is personal leverage?

A. The debt and guarantees that sit on you as an individual rather than inside a project company, which can reach assets unrelated to any one deal.

Q. What is a trigger in a risk register?

A. A defined, observable condition that tells the risk owner it is time to carry out the planned response.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender looks at a young developer and sees a company that is one person deep. That observation shows up in the term sheet as a key-principal clause, a requirement for personal guarantees, a larger interest or operating reserve, or a lower loan amount. You are already paying for key-person risk. The question is whether you pay in the cheapest currency.

How lenders price dependence on one person

In plain English: if the lender thinks the project could stall without you, it protects itself, and you pay for the protection.

The professional framing lists the levers. A key-principal clause turns your absence into a potential default. A personal guarantee makes your estate stand behind the loan. A reserve requirement holds back cash the project cannot use. A lower loan-to-cost ratio forces more equity in. Each is a commercial term, negotiated deal by deal, not a standard. And each costs money: a reserve has a carrying cost, extra equity has a required return, and a default clause has an expected cost equal to its probability times its damage.

A worked example, hypothetical round numbers. A lender offers a 15,000,000 dollar loan with a 600,000 dollar additional reserve held for the life of the loan because the sponsor is a single principal. Equity that could otherwise earn, say, 15 percent a year in the project is tied up. The cost is 600,000 times 15 percent, about 90,000 dollars a year of forgone return. Now suppose key-person life and disability cover on the principal, assigned to the lender, costs about 12,000 dollars a year for this person, and the lender agrees to drop the extra reserve in exchange. The insurance is cheaper by about 78,000 dollars a year. Whether a lender will make that trade is a negotiation, not a right; the example shows why it is worth proposing.

Protecting debt service

In plain English: if you are the reason the project performs, your absence can push the debt service coverage ratio below the covenant, and insurance can fill the gap.

The professional framing returns to the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) from Week 36: net operating income divided by annual debt service. A stabilised building with a capable property manager does not depend on one person. A building in lease-up, or a company where the founder personally drives sales, can.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A building is in lease-up. Projected net operating income for the year is 1,300,000 dollars and debt service is 1,000,000 dollars, a DSCR of 1.30. The covenant minimum is 1.20, a commercial term. If the principal cannot work for six months during lease-up, the sponsor estimates leasing slows and NOI falls by 150,000 dollars to 1,150,000 dollars. DSCR drops to 1.15, a breach. To restore 1.20, NOI would need to be 1,200,000 dollars, so the shortfall is 50,000 dollars. Many loans allow a cure by depositing cash or paying down principal; the cure terms are in your agreement. A business-overhead or key-person disability benefit that pays the company 25,000 dollars a month for six months would provide 150,000 dollars, enough to cure the gap with room to spare.

Say that out loud now.

What the premium buys, and what it does not

Insurance transfers a defined financial loss. It does not replace judgement, relationships or the time it takes the lender to trust a successor. So the money from a policy should be pre-assigned to jobs: repay or reduce the guaranteed exposure, fund the buyout, pay for an interim leader and cover the slowdown. Cover sized to the loan alone ignores the cost of keeping the project moving. Cover sized to a round number ignores everything.

Premiums depend on age, health, amount, definition of the cover and the insurer, and they generally rise with age. Buying when young and healthy is cheaper, but buying cover you do not need is still waste. Size it to the map, then review it.

How the best do it

Large, well-run contractors and developers manage key-person risk mainly by not having it: every critical role is staffed at least two deep, signing authorities are documented with named deputies, client relationships are held by teams rather than individuals, and succession is planned for senior roles years ahead. Insurance is the backstop, not the plan. The practice a small developer can copy is a named deputy for each of your own critical roles, written down, who attends key meetings so the lender and the contractor already know them.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's Wealth Ledger for this subject. On your personal balance sheet, list each policy that protects you or your obligations: its face amount, its annual premium, who owns it, who receives the money and which obligation it funds. Add the obligations map from Day 2 opposite it, so the two columns can be compared line by line. A policy with no obligation opposite it is a candidate for cancelling; an obligation with no policy or reserve opposite it is a hole. Remember that a policy owned by a company is a company asset, not yours, and that its cash value, if any, may be reachable by that company's creditors.

A licensed adviser is required before you act. This lesson teaches concepts; it recommends no insurer, policy or product.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is paying for key-person risk twice, through restrictive loan terms and through premiums, because nobody offered the lender the trade. The control is to price the lender's protection in dollars a year and put a funded alternative on the table before the term sheet is signed.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking insurance is a pure cost. Compared with a reserve, extra equity or a default risk, it is often the cheapest way to carry the same risk.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught that guarantees and carve-outs decide personal exposure on a construction loan, and that a personal guarantee can bind your estate after death. This lesson prices the other side: what it costs to make sure your estate can meet that guarantee without a fire sale.

Recap

Lenders price single-person dependence through clauses, guarantees, reserves and lower leverage. On hypothetical numbers, a 600,000 dollar reserve cost about 90,000 dollars a year against a 12,000 dollar premium. Disability cover can cure a DSCR breach during lease-up. The best firms remove key-person risk by depth; insurance backs that up.

Next: LEX on The Rules: insurable interest, disclosure, ownership, beneficiaries and assignment.
checklist: I have priced, in dollars a year, every lender protection that exists because I am a single principal.
I have offered the lender a funded alternative before the term sheet is signed.
I know my DSCR covenant and the cure terms in each loan.
Policy proceeds are pre-assigned to specific jobs.
Each critical role I hold has a named deputy who is known to the lender.
My Wealth Ledger matches each policy to the obligation it funds.
I remember that a company-owned policy is a company asset.
head: Field checklist
speak: Key-person risk has a price whether or not I insure it. Lenders price dependence on one person through a key-principal clause, personal guarantees, extra reserves or a lower loan amount. On hypothetical numbers, a 600,000 dollar reserve held for the life of a loan costs about 90,000 dollars a year in forgone equity return, while key-person cover assigned to the lender might cost 12,000 dollars a year. That trade is worth proposing. Disability can hit debt service too. A lease-up building with a DSCR of 1.30 against a 1.20 covenant drops to 1.15 if leasing slows while I cannot work, and a disability benefit paid to the company can cure the gap. Insurance transfers money, not judgement, so proceeds are pre-assigned to jobs. The best firms remove key-person risk by staffing every critical role two deep and use insurance as the backstop.
terms: Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) — net operating income divided by annual debt service; lenders set a minimum as a covenant.
Business-overhead disability cover — insurance that pays a business's fixed costs for a period if its owner cannot work.
Assignment of a policy — a transfer of some or all rights under an insurance policy, often to a lender as security.

hostile.q: We require a 600,000 dollar additional reserve because the sponsor is one person. Why should we drop it?
hostile.a: Because it protects against a specific event, my death or disability, and I can protect you against that event more directly. I will provide key-person life and disability cover on me in an amount you set, assigned to you to the extent of the loan, with the insurer acknowledging the assignment. You keep the protection, and the project keeps its equity working. I can also name a deputy with documented authority.

title: An Insurance Policy Is a Contract: Disclosure, Ownership and Assignment
summary: An insurance policy is a contract with unusual rules: you must have an insurable interest, you must disclose what matters, and the owner, the insured and the beneficiary can be three different people. This lesson teaches how to read a policy and what can make it fail when it is needed.
body:
An insurance policy is a contract, and like any contract it can fail at the moment you rely on it. Most failures come from three places: what you did not disclose, who owns it, and what the definitions actually say.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 87?

A. Never invest where the manager, the custodian and the record keeper are the same party or under the same control; require independent custody and an auditor you have checked yourself.

Q. What makes a guarantee dangerous on a personal balance sheet?

A. It is a contingent liability that does not appear as debt until it is called, so the balance sheet looks stronger than it is.

Q. What does a Monte Carlo analysis add to a contingency estimate?

A. It runs many simulated outcomes from ranges of cost and duration, producing a probability distribution, so contingency can be set to a chosen confidence level rather than a flat percentage.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you read construction contracts for their notice clauses and their definitions, because that is where claims are won or lost. Insurance is the same. The premium and the face amount are the commercial terms; the definitions, the exclusions and the disclosure obligations decide whether the money arrives. This lesson teaches concepts. Insurance law differs by jurisdiction and policy wording; verify every point against the primary source and your policy before you rely on it.

Insurable interest and the three parties

In plain English: you can only insure a life or a risk if its loss would genuinely harm you, and the person who owns the policy, the person whose life is covered and the person who gets paid can all be different.

The professional framing names the parties. The policy owner controls the contract: pays the premium, can change beneficiaries where permitted, and can cancel or assign it. The life insured is the person whose death or disability triggers payment. The beneficiary receives the proceeds. Most legal systems require the owner to have an insurable interest in the life insured, typically a family relationship or a financial dependence such as an employer in a key employee or a partner in a co-owner, usually tested when the policy is taken out. The rules vary; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A worked example, hypothetical. A company owns a policy on its founder, pays the premium and is named beneficiary. That is key-person insurance: the money goes to the company, where the company's creditors may be able to reach it. A different design has each partner own a policy on the other, for a cross-purchase buy-sell, so the money lands with the survivor who must buy the shares. Same life, same amount, different owner and beneficiary, and a completely different result. That choice has tax consequences a tax adviser must design.

Disclosure: the duty that makes or breaks the claim

In plain English: when you apply, you must tell the insurer the truth about anything that matters to their decision, and if you do not, they may be able to refuse to pay.

The professional framing comes from the principle of utmost good faith: insurance contracts have traditionally required the applicant to disclose material facts the insurer would want to know, such as health history, risky activities and other cover. Many jurisdictions now limit the duty to answering the insurer's questions honestly, and many policies include a contestability period during which the insurer can investigate and void the policy for misrepresentation; after it, the policy is harder to challenge except for fraud. The length and scope of these rules vary; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Say that out loud now.

A second worked example, hypothetical. An applicant answers no to a question about treatment for a heart condition in the past five years, forgetting a short course of medication. Two years later he dies of an unrelated cause. Within the contestability period the insurer reviews records, finds the omission and seeks to rescind the policy, returning premiums instead of paying the benefit. Whether it succeeds depends on the law and on whether the fact was material. The family's case now rests on a disputed form, not on a contract. The control is cheap: gather your medical records before applying and answer from documents, not memory.

Definitions, exclusions and renewal

In plain English: a disability policy pays only for the disability it defines, and the words decide almost everything.

The professional framing distinguishes an own-occupation definition, which pays if you cannot do your own occupation, from an any-occupation definition, which pays only if you cannot do any reasonable occupation for your education and experience. A developer who could still work as a consultant may be unable to run projects and yet not be disabled under an any-occupation test. Read also the elimination period, the waiting time before benefits start; the benefit period, how long benefits last; partial or residual benefits for reduced work; exclusions; and renewal terms. A policy described as non-cancellable or guaranteed renewable limits the insurer's right to cancel or reprice, in different ways. These are policy terms; read your own.

Assignment and beneficiary designations

A lender may ask for a collateral assignment of a policy, giving it the right to be paid from the proceeds up to the amount owed, with any balance going to the named beneficiary. Insist that the assignment is limited to the debt, released when the loan is repaid, and acknowledged in writing by the insurer, because an insurer that has not recorded the assignment may pay the wrong person. Beneficiary designations, in many systems, pass outside the will and can override it. Tessa will return to that in the trust weeks; for now, treat every designation as part of your estate plan and review it whenever circumstances change.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, for ownership, assignment and buy-sell design; licensed insurance adviser, for the policy wording; tax adviser, for the treatment of premiums and proceeds.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a policy that is voidable for non-disclosure or that defines disability so narrowly it never pays for the job you actually do. The control is to apply from documents, keep a copy of the full application, and read the definitions and exclusions before you sign.

The beginner's mistake

Reading only the face amount and the premium, and leaving the owner and beneficiary fields to the agent. Those two fields decide who controls the policy and who gets the money.

Callback

In Week 77, LEX and Marco taught that conditions precedent and time bars decide construction claims regardless of merit. Insurance claims work the same way: notice requirements, proof of loss, the elimination period and the contestability window are conditions you meet or lose on.

Recap

Owner, life insured and beneficiary can be different people, and the choice decides who controls and receives the money. Disclose honestly from documents. Read the disability definition, waiting and benefit periods, exclusions and renewal. Limit any assignment to the debt and get the insurer's written acknowledgment.

Next: Warrick on The Numbers: reverse engineering the cover you need from the obligations it must fund.
checklist: I know who owns, who is insured under, and who benefits from every policy.
Ownership and beneficiary match the agreement each policy funds.
I answer applications from documents, and I keep a copy of the full application.
I know whether my disability cover uses an own-occupation or any-occupation definition.
I know the elimination period, benefit period and exclusions.
Any lender assignment is limited to the debt, releasable and acknowledged by the insurer.
Beneficiary designations are reviewed with my will whenever circumstances change.
head: Field checklist
speak: An insurance policy is a contract, and it can fail exactly when I need it. The owner controls it, the life insured is the person covered, and the beneficiary gets paid, and they can be three different people. That choice decides who controls the money and whose creditors might reach it. The owner generally needs an insurable interest in the life insured. Disclosure is the second risk: I must answer the insurer's questions truthfully, and many policies have a contestability period during which a misstatement can void the cover, so I apply from my medical records, not memory. Third, definitions. A disability policy with an any-occupation definition may not pay if I can still consult but cannot run projects. I read the waiting period, the benefit period, exclusions and renewal terms. If a lender takes an assignment, it is limited to the debt and acknowledged by the insurer in writing.
terms: Insurable interest — a genuine financial or family stake in the life or risk insured, generally required for a valid policy.
Contestability period — a period after a policy starts during which the insurer may investigate and challenge it for misstatement.
Own-occupation definition — a disability definition that pays if the insured cannot perform their own occupation.

hostile.q: Your disability policy pays only if you cannot work in any occupation. You could still teach or consult. Why do you think it protects your projects?
hostile.a: I don't, and that is the gap I have flagged. The current policy protects household income at a basic level. For the company I am arranging cover with an own-occupation definition, or business-overhead cover that pays the company's fixed costs if I cannot run projects, with the definitions reviewed by my lawyer before I sign.

title: Reverse Engineering the Cover: From the Obligation Back to the Policy
summary: Start from the outcome: what must be paid, to whom and by when if a hypothetical developer dies or cannot work. Work backward through existing resources, taxes and waiting periods to the face amount and monthly benefit needed. Every step has units.
body:
The right amount of insurance is not a multiple of income or a round number. It is what remains when you take every obligation a death or disability would trigger, subtract the resources that would already meet it, and adjust for tax and timing.

Recall

Q. What is human capital?

A. The present value of all future earnings from a person's work, often the largest asset early in a career and absent from every statement.

Q. Why does leverage held personally magnify a loss more than its size suggests?

A. Because the debt stays fixed while the asset falls, so the loss lands entirely on your equity, and a personal guarantee can extend it beyond the asset itself.

Q. In risk management, what is the first response to a contractor default?

A. Secure the site and the records, give the notices the contract and any bond require, and assess the cost to complete before choosing a replacement path.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even week, so we reverse engineer. Most people choose cover by starting with a premium they can afford and seeing what it buys. Developers should work the other way, as they do with a land price: start from what the outcome must be and work back to the number that delivers it. All figures below are hypothetical round numbers for a hypothetical developer, for arithmetic only.

Part 1: life cover, starting from the outcome

The outcome we want: if the developer dies, within 90 days the company can satisfy its lender, buy out his estate's shares, and fund a replacement leader, and his household can carry on.

Step 1: list the company obligations a death triggers.

  1. Buy-sell price for his half of the company, by formula: 2,500,000 dollars.
  2. Guaranteed loan exposure the lender requires reduced on his death, under a negotiated release: 1,500,000 dollars.
  3. Interim leader and slowdown cost for 12 months: 300,000 dollars.
  4. Total company obligations: 4,300,000 dollars.

Step 2: subtract resources that would already meet them.

  1. Company cash available without breaking any covenant: 400,000 dollars.
  2. Net company need: 4,300,000 minus 400,000 equals 3,900,000 dollars.

Step 3: list household obligations, separately, because they are paid to different people.

  1. Household spending of 90,000 dollars a year for 15 years. At a hypothetical real return of 3 percent a year on the invested proceeds, the present value is about 1,074,000 dollars.
  2. Personal debts to clear: 250,000 dollars.
  3. Total household need: about 1,324,000 dollars.
  4. Less personal liquid assets the household would keep: 300,000 dollars.
  5. Net household need: about 1,024,000 dollars, rounded to 1,050,000 dollars to allow for costs.

Step 4: adjust for tax. Whether life insurance proceeds are taxed depends on the jurisdiction, the ownership and the purpose; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. If, hypothetically, proceeds would be tax-free, no gross-up is needed. If any part would be taxed, gross it up: a need of 1,050,000 dollars taxed at a hypothetical 20 percent requires 1,050,000 divided by 0.80, which is 1,312,500 dollars.

Result, assuming tax-free proceeds: about 3,900,000 dollars of key-person and buy-sell cover, structured as the agreements require, and about 1,050,000 dollars of personal cover. That is two policies with two jobs, not one large round number.

Say that out loud now.

Part 2: disability cover, starting from the outcome

The outcome we want: if he cannot work, his household keeps 10,000 dollars a month after tax, and the company can carry its fixed costs and pay an interim leader.

Step 1: the household gap.

  1. Required after-tax income: 10,000 dollars a month.
  2. Income that continues without him working, such as rent from a personally held unit: 2,500 dollars a month after tax.
  3. Gap: 7,500 dollars a month after tax.

Step 2: the tax gross-up. Whether disability benefits are taxed depends largely on who paid the premiums and how; verify that against the primary source. If, hypothetically, benefits would be taxed at 30 percent, the gross benefit needed is 7,500 divided by 0.70, about 10,700 dollars a month. If they would be tax-free, 7,500 dollars a month is enough. The structure of the premium payment can be worth more than the premium.

Step 3: the insurer's ceiling. Insurers commonly cap individual disability benefits at a share of earned income, a commercial practice that varies by insurer. Suppose this developer's earned income is 180,000 dollars a year and the hypothetical cap is 60 percent: 108,000 dollars a year, or 9,000 dollars a month. A taxable need of 10,700 dollars exceeds the cap; a tax-free need of 7,500 dollars fits within it. This is a real design constraint, and it often pushes the remaining protection onto reserves.

Step 4: the waiting period. With a 90-day elimination period, benefits start after three months. The household must carry three months alone: 3 times 10,000 is 30,000 dollars of liquid reserve, sitting in the liquidity floor from Week 7. A longer waiting period lowers the premium and raises the reserve. Choose the pair together.

Step 5: the company side. Fixed costs of 35,000 dollars a month plus an interim leader at 15,000 dollars a month is 50,000 dollars a month. Over a 12-month benefit period that is 600,000 dollars. Business-overhead or key-person disability cover sized to that, owned by the company, is the job.

Part 3: reconciling with the obligations map

Write each result opposite its obligation on the Day 2 map: company life cover against the buyout and guarantee; personal life cover against the household; personal disability against the household gap; company disability against fixed costs. Then review it whenever the company value, the loan or the household changes. A buy-sell price that grows each year needs cover that grows with it.

A licensed adviser is required before you act. This lesson teaches concepts; it recommends no insurer, policy or product.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is sizing from the premium instead of from the obligation, which produces cover that is affordable and inadequate. The control is to start every sizing from the written list of obligations and to let the premium be the last number calculated, not the first.

The beginner's mistake

Mixing company and household needs into one personal policy. The money then lands in the wrong place, owned by the wrong person, and the buyout or the loan goes unfunded while the household receives more than it needs.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage reverse engineered a deal from public information to find the implied land price. The method here is the same: fix the required outcome, then solve backward for the one unknown. There it was land; here it is cover.

Recap

Start from what must be paid. Subtract existing resources. Gross up for tax only where proceeds would be taxed. Respect the insurer's benefit cap and fund the waiting period from reserves. Keep company and household cover separate, each opposite its obligation.

Next: Priya in The Room: the lender who demands an assignment of your key-person policy.
checklist: I size cover from obligations, not from a premium I can afford.
I keep company needs and household needs separate.
I subtract existing resources before calculating cover.
I know whether proceeds and benefits would be taxed, and gross up only where they would.
I know the insurer's benefit cap and plan around it.
My liquidity floor covers the elimination period.
I review cover whenever the company value, loans or household change.
head: Field checklist
speak: Reverse engineering cover starts from the outcome. For life cover, I list what a death triggers in the company: on hypothetical numbers, a 2.5 million dollar buyout, 1.5 million of guaranteed debt to reduce, and 300,000 for an interim leader, 4.3 million in all. Subtract 400,000 of usable company cash, and the company needs about 3.9 million. The household is separate: spending and debts less personal assets leaves about 1.05 million. If proceeds would be taxed, I gross up; if not, I don't. For disability, a 7,500 dollar monthly after-tax gap becomes about 10,700 if benefits are taxed at 30 percent, which may exceed the insurer's cap, so premium structure matters. A 90-day waiting period means 30,000 dollars must sit in reserves. The company separately needs about 600,000 for a year of fixed costs and a leader. Premium is the last number, never the first.
terms: Elimination period — the waiting time after a disability begins before benefits start.
Benefit period — the maximum length of time a disability policy will pay benefits.
Gross-up — increasing a benefit so that the amount left after tax equals the amount actually needed.

hostile.q: You want 3.9 million dollars of company cover on one person. Isn't that over-insured for a company your size?
hostile.a: It is sized to three written obligations: the buy-sell price, the guaranteed debt the lender requires reduced, and twelve months of interim leadership, less the cash the company could use without breaking a covenant. If any of those falls, the cover falls with it at the next annual review. I can show you each line and the document behind it.

title: The Lender Who Wants Your Policy
summary: A credit officer makes key-person cover, assigned to the bank, a condition of the loan. This lesson scripts the negotiation: the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state. It closes with the monthly thread on founder health.
body:
When a lender asks for your key-person policy, it is asking a fair question in a negotiable form. Agree to the principle quickly, then negotiate the amount, the scope of the assignment and the release.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 88?

A. Before any loan closes, every death or disability that would trigger a default, a buyout or a lost guarantee must be funded by insurance or reserves, tied in writing to the document that needs it.

Q. What makes a position "too big" in personal capital allocation?

A. When a single loss on it would change your life or prevent you meeting other obligations, whatever its expected return.

Q. What does N-minus-1 thinking from grid operations teach about project risk?

A. That a system should keep operating after the loss of any single element. On a project, no single person, supplier or contractor failure should stop the whole job.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender's request for insurance is not an insult. It is the lender applying N-minus-1 thinking to you. If you resist the principle you look like someone who has not thought about your own mortality. If you accept every detail you may hand over more control of a policy than the debt justifies. The skill is to agree fast and negotiate carefully.

The scene

A hypothetical scene. A credit officer has your term sheet for a 12,000,000 dollar construction loan. She says: "Credit committee will require key-person life cover on you of 12,000,000 dollars, collaterally assigned to the bank, as a condition precedent to first draw." You have already mapped your obligations and have company cover of 4,000,000 dollars on you for a buy-sell and an interim leader.

The lines to say

  • "That's a reasonable concern. The project shouldn't depend on one person's health, and I've already planned for it."
  • "Help me understand the amount. Is the committee covering the full loan, or the exposure during construction before the building can be completed by someone else?"
  • "I'd propose cover equal to your exposure at peak, reducing as the loan reduces, assigned to the extent of the outstanding debt, with any balance to the company."
  • "We'll want the assignment released automatically on repayment, and acknowledged in writing by the insurer."
  • "I already hold company cover for our buy-sell. I'd like to keep that separate, so the lender and the buyout aren't competing for the same money."
  • "If cover on me is a condition, can the additional operating reserve come down in exchange?"

The lines never to say

  • "I'm healthy, I don't need it." Health today says nothing about next year, and it tells the lender you have not planned.
  • "Take whatever policy you want." You may hand over the buy-sell cover and leave your partner and estate unfunded.
  • "Can we deal with that after closing?" A condition precedent means no first draw until it is met, and insurance underwriting can take weeks.
  • "Just put it on my existing policy." Assigning a policy that already funds something else creates two claims on one pot.

Say that out loud now.

The question behind the question

The stated question is about insurance. The question behind it is: "If you disappear, can this project still be finished and repaid?" Insurance is one answer. A named deputy with documented authority, a strong contractor with a completion bond, and a lender's monitor who already knows the project are others. Answer the real question in full: "Here is the cover, and here is who runs the project the day after." The more credible your succession plan, the less insurance the lender needs to feel safe.

When she asks for cover on the full loan amount, the question behind that may be committee habit rather than analysis. A full-amount requirement ignores that the building itself, once substantially complete, is security. Offer a reducing amount tied to exposure, and give her a one-page note she can take to committee that explains why.

When to stay silent

After you propose a reducing amount and a trade on the reserve, stop. Let her consider it. Do not start defending the number before she has objected to it. Silence after a proposal tells her it is a real proposal, not an opening bid you are nervous about.

Holding your state

Conversations about your own death and disability are uncomfortable, and discomfort makes people either joke or concede. Do neither. Treat it as a risk item, like soil conditions: you have investigated it, you have a plan, and here are the numbers. If you feel your pace quicken, slow it deliberately, shorten your sentences and refer to your written obligations map. Composure here signals the same thing to the lender that it does in a cost meeting: this sponsor has thought ahead.

Founder health: the monthly thread

Insurance underwriting forces a question most founders avoid: what is your actual health? Applying usually means a medical questionnaire and sometimes an examination and blood tests. Treat that as a free annual audit rather than an obstacle. Shift work, irregular meals, poor sleep and long drives, which Kema covered in Week 4, show up in blood pressure, weight and blood results. Your premiums, your capacity and your judgement all depend on them.

A practical habit, labelled practitioner habit rather than research: book an annual check-up in the same month every year, keep the results in your records, and apply for or review cover with those documents in hand. Ask your doctor what one change would matter most for you. Check with your doctor before changing exercise, diet or sleep routines, and never act on general guidance in place of their advice.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is conceding an assignment of the only policy that funds your buy-sell, so that on your death the lender is paid and your partner and estate are not. The control is separate policies for separate jobs, an assignment limited to the debt, and an obligations map that shows the lender why.

The beginner's mistake

Arguing against the principle of key-person cover, which makes the sponsor look unprepared, instead of agreeing to it and negotiating the amount, the scope and the release.

Callback

In Week 67, Priya taught what to ask a lender for, what to trade and when to walk. This meeting is a small version of that: accept the lender's concern, trade cover for a lower reserve, and keep the parts of the structure that protect other people you owe.

Recap

Agree to the principle. Negotiate a reducing amount tied to exposure, an assignment limited to the debt, an automatic release and insurer acknowledgment. Keep buy-sell cover separate. Answer the real question with a succession plan. Stay silent after you propose.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap, with Cole's Auditor's Chair: reading a hypothetical insurance schedule as a hostile auditor would.
checklist: I agree to the principle of key-person cover without hesitation.
I propose cover tied to the lender's exposure, reducing as the loan reduces.
Any assignment is limited to the debt and released automatically on repayment.
The insurer acknowledges the assignment in writing.
Buy-sell cover stays separate from lender cover.
I present a named deputy and a succession plan alongside the policy.
I start underwriting early so a condition precedent does not delay first draw.
I book an annual check-up and keep the results with my records.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a lender asks for key-person cover assigned to the bank, I agree to the principle at once, because the project should not depend on one person's health. Then I negotiate three things. The amount: cover tied to the lender's exposure during construction, reducing as the loan reduces, rather than the full loan by habit. The scope: an assignment limited to the outstanding debt, with any balance to the company, released automatically on repayment and acknowledged by the insurer. And separation: my buy-sell cover stays separate so the lender and my partner are not claiming the same money. I answer the question behind the question with a named deputy and a succession plan. I may trade the cover for a lower reserve. After I propose, I stay silent. I start underwriting early, and I treat the medical as an annual health audit, checking changes with my doctor.
terms: Collateral assignment — an assignment giving a lender the right to policy proceeds up to the amount owed, with the balance to the beneficiary.
Condition precedent — something that must be satisfied before an obligation, such as the first loan advance, arises.
Succession plan — a written plan naming who takes over critical roles and authority if a person cannot continue.

hostile.q: Committee wants cover equal to the full 12,000,000 dollar loan. Why should we accept less?
hostile.a: Because your exposure to my death is highest during construction, before the building can be completed by someone else, and it falls as work is completed and the loan is repaid. I'll provide cover equal to peak exposure, reducing on a schedule we agree, assigned to the extent of the debt, plus a named deputy and a completion bond on the contractor. I'll put that in a one-page note for committee.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 88 Review: Insuring the Asset You Cannot Diversify
summary: Six questions on life, disability and key-person insurance, a recap of the week, Cole's Auditor's Chair on a hypothetical insurance schedule and buy-sell clause, and a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: list every obligation your death or disability would trigger, fund each one with reserves, insurance or a change in structure, and make sure the right person owns and receives every policy.

Recall

Q. In the Day 3 example, why was key-person cover cheaper than the lender's extra reserve?

A. The 600,000 dollar reserve cost about 90,000 dollars a year in forgone equity return, while the cover assigned to the lender cost about 12,000 dollars a year, on hypothetical numbers.

Q. What does concentration risk mean for a developer's net worth?

A. That too much of it depends on one asset, market or person, so one failure changes everything.

Q. What is contractor default risk, and what is the first control?

A. The risk that the contractor cannot finish or pay its trades. The first control is prequalification of its finances, backed by security such as bonds, and payment that never runs ahead of work in place.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you cannot diversify yourself. You can only transfer the financial consequences of losing yourself, or build a company that does not need you every day. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can design that protection with your advisers instead of being sold it. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is human capital, and why does it matter for insurance?

Answer: The present value of your future earnings. Early in a career it is often your largest asset, and insurance protects the people and obligations that depend on it.

Question 2. Name the three covers and the question each answers.

Answer: Life insurance: what if I die? Disability insurance: what if I cannot work? Key-person insurance: what happens to the business if either occurs?

Question 3. What three obligations failed in the Day 2 composite, and what is Rule 88?

Answer: The buy-sell, the key-principal replacement and the guarantees. Rule 88: before any loan closes, every death or disability trigger must be funded and the funding tied in writing to the document that needs it.

Question 4. Why do owner, life insured and beneficiary matter?

Answer: The owner controls the policy and the beneficiary receives the money, so together they decide whether proceeds reach the buyout, the lender, the household or a company's creditors.

Question 5. Why does the definition of disability matter so much?

Answer: An any-occupation definition may not pay if you can still do some work, even if you cannot run projects; an own-occupation definition pays if you cannot do your own job.

Question 6. How do you size cover?

Answer: From obligations backward: list what must be paid, subtract existing resources, gross up only for tax that would apply, respect the insurer's cap, and fund the waiting period from reserves. The premium is the last number.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Warrick, with Priya, framed insurance as architecture protecting human capital. Ford and Roman took a composite case of an unfunded buy-sell and a key-principal default, giving Rule 88. Priya priced key-person risk against loan terms and showed disability cover curing a DSCR breach. LEX taught insurable interest, disclosure, definitions and assignment. Warrick reverse engineered life and disability cover from obligations. Priya negotiated a lender's assignment request.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 88 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical insurance schedule as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Insurance Schedule, Company and Principals. Policy 1: life cover on Partner A, 2,000,000 dollars, owner Partner A, beneficiary Partner A's spouse; purpose: buy-sell funding. Policy 2: life cover on Partner B, 2,000,000 dollars, owner the Company, beneficiary the Company; purpose: buy-sell funding; collaterally assigned to the Lender, no limit stated. Policy 3: disability cover on Partner A, any-occupation definition, 180-day elimination period. Buy-sell clause: survivor purchases at formula value, currently 3,400,000 dollars per half, payable within 12 months. Last reviewed: three years ago.

The defects. First, Policy 1 names Partner A's spouse as beneficiary, so on A's death the money goes to the household, not to the survivor who must buy the shares; the buyout is unfunded. Second, both policies are 2,000,000 dollars against a buyout of 3,400,000 dollars per half, so even correctly structured they leave 1,400,000 dollars short. Third, the two policies are structured differently for the same purpose, which suggests nobody designed them together. Fourth, Policy 2 is assigned to the lender with no limit, so the lender may take all of the money meant for the buyout. Fifth, there is no disability cover on Partner B at all, and the buy-sell does not say what happens on disability. Sixth, Policy 3's any-occupation definition and 180-day wait may leave Partner A without benefits for months, or at all. Seventh, the schedule was last reviewed three years ago while the formula value has clearly grown.

Then the auditor asks for evidence: the policies themselves, the beneficiary confirmations from the insurers, the assignment document and the insurer's acknowledgment, the latest formula valuation, and the board minute approving the company-owned policy. A schedule that cannot produce those in an hour describes intentions, not protection.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a new partner who asks, "Why are we spending money on insurance when we're both healthy?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because our company, our loans and our families depend on two people, and health today tells us nothing about next year. Our shareholder agreement makes the survivor buy out the other's estate at formula value within a year. Our loan treats either of us dying or being unable to work as an event the bank must approve. And we both sign guarantees that bind our estates. None of those obligations can be met from the cash we hold. So we map them, size cover to each one, keep company cover and household cover separate, make sure each policy is owned and paid to the right party, and limit any bank assignment to the debt. We use own-occupation disability cover, because we could still consult and yet be unable to run a project. And we review it all every year with our lawyer, tax adviser and a licensed insurance adviser."

Score yourself. Did you lead with the obligations rather than the policies? Did you mention disability? Did you mention ownership and beneficiaries? Did you finish inside two minutes?

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a schedule of policies that looks complete and pays the wrong people, the wrong amounts, at the wrong time. The control is the obligations map, matched line by line to each policy's owner, beneficiary and amount, reviewed every year.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the insurance schedule as a filing task for an assistant, rather than as part of the capital structure that a principal must read.

Callback

In Week 79, Priya and Marco taught project insurance: builder's risk, liability, owner-controlled programs and waiver of subrogation. That protected the building. This week protected the people behind it. Both are architecture: decide what must survive, then insure the gap.

Recap

Map the obligations. Separate company from household. Size from obligations backward. Check owner, beneficiary, definition, waiting period and assignment. Review every year. Rule 88 ties each trigger to its funding.

Next: Omar, with Tessa, on First Principles: asset protection, ring-fencing and why timing decides everything.
checklist: What is human capital, and why does it matter for insurance?
Name the three covers and the question each answers.
What three obligations failed in the Day 2 composite, and what is Rule 88?
Why do owner, life insured and beneficiary matter?
Why does the definition of disability matter so much?
How do you size cover?
head: The six questions
speak: This week was about insuring the one asset I cannot diversify: my ability to earn, sign and lead. Life cover answers what happens if I die, disability cover what happens if I cannot work, and key-person cover what happens to the business. Lenders price dependence on one person through clauses, guarantees and reserves, and cover can be the cheaper way to carry that risk. The Day 2 composite gave Rule 88: every death or disability trigger must be funded and tied in writing to the document that needs it before the loan closes. A policy is a contract: owner, life insured and beneficiary decide where the money goes, disclosure must be honest and documented, and the definition of disability decides whether it pays. I size cover from obligations backward, keep company and household cover separate, limit any lender assignment to the debt, and review everything every year with licensed advisers.
terms: Obligations map — a written list of every payment a person's death or disability would trigger, with amount, deadline and funding source.
Cross-purchase arrangement — a buy-sell design in which each owner holds cover on the other so the survivor receives the money to buy the shares.
Beneficiary designation — the named recipient of insurance proceeds, which in many systems passes outside the will.

hostile.q: Your schedule shows the buy-sell policy on Partner A paying his spouse. If A dies tomorrow, how does Partner B buy the shares?
hostile.a: He can't, on that schedule, and that is a defect I'm fixing. The buy-sell cover must be owned and payable so the money reaches the party obliged to buy, and it must match the current formula price, which it doesn't. Household cover will be a separate policy. I'll have the corrected structure reviewed by our lawyer and tax adviser and confirmed by the insurers in writing.
